summary:
Niger stands under Nigeria's national framework, which applies here as it does elsewhere in the country. The findings below are specific to Niger State.

Niger State is one of the twelve northern states Human Rights Watch identified in its 2004 survey as having adopted Sharia criminal provisions, alongside Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. The wave traced from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force from 27 January 2000, and those provisions remain in force.

Niger State's own instrument is the Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (HB.4/2000), signed 22 February 2000, gazetted as Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8 of 9 March 2000, and in operation from 4 May 2000. It amends the Penal Code of 1960 rather than replacing it: it defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68, while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies. The result is a distinct criminal track for Muslim defendants, so an outed Muslim visitor in Niger State stands under a harsher parallel frame than federal law alone.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) sets out the hybrid legal system, the twelve-state Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women, and notes the limits of available arrest data.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement in Niger State is documented through the same raid pattern seen across the northern bloc, though the specific mass arrests catalogued in the parent record occurred in other states. The state-level statutory proof above establishes the legal layer; the parent record carries the national enforcement picture.

The 2004 Human Rights Watch survey places Niger State within a twelve-state bloc, so the northern-bloc criminalisation claim applies here as a group finding rather than as a Niger State-specific enforcement count.
localsOnly:
Section 68A applies its harsher burden of proof and punishment only to Muslim defendants; non-Muslim residents of Niger State remain under the ordinary Penal Code punishments for the same conduct. The amendment is a state statute gazetted in Niger State's own official record, so it binds residents directly and independently of federal legislation.

The amendment's definition of 'adultery' to encompass sodomy extends the reach of the state's adultery provisions to same-sex conduct, and the amended section 68 caning paragraph carries amputation as an added penalty where the Islamic evidentiary standard is met.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document any Niger State-specific arrest, prosecution or violence incident under the Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000; enforcement frequency in this state is unresolved from these sources.

No source in this inventory records a Niger State court decision applying section 68A to a sodomy or adultery charge, so the practical application of the harsher track is not sourced here.

The UK Home Office note's observation about the limits of available arrest data applies to Nigeria nationally; no state-level arrest statistics for Niger State appear in this inventory.
